final_proof:
By definition, the set of $p$-adic integers, denoted $\mathbb{Z}_p$, is a subset of the $p$-adic numbers $\mathbb{Q}_p$.

Every $p$-adic integer can be uniquely represented as a formal power series of the form:
$$ x = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n p^n $$
where each coefficient $a_n$ is an integer satisfying $0 \le a_n \le p-1$.

Thus, there is a natural bijection between the set $\mathbb{Z}_p$ and the set of all infinite sequences $(a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots)$ taking values in the finite set $\{0, 1, \dots, p-1\}$.
The set of all such sequences is equivalent to the set of functions from the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, p-1\}$.

The cardinality of the set $\{0, 1, \dots, p-1\}$ is $p$. Therefore, the cardinality of the set of all such sequences is $p^{\aleph_0}$.
Since $p$ is a prime number, we have $p \ge 2$, which implies:
$$ p^{\aleph_0} = 2^{\aleph_0} = \mathfrak{c} $$
where $\mathfrak{c}$ denotes the cardinality of the continuum. Since $\mathfrak{c} > \aleph_0$, the set $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is uncountable.

Because $\mathbb{Z}_p \subseteq \mathbb{Q}_p$, the set of $p$-adic numbers $\mathbb{Q}_p$ contains an uncountable subset and is therefore itself an uncountable set. $\blacksquare$
